images.title: Boxes of four bangles
images.purpose: Pose the question of whether every fraction greater than one can be a mixed number, using 11/4 as a sample: full boxes give the whole part and the bangles left give the fraction part.
images.composition: Two full boxes and one part box in a row with wide gaps, the sample equation below, and one question line under it.
images.exact_structure: Three identical small open boxes in a row, each with room for exactly 4 bangles side by side. First 2 boxes: exactly 4 round bangles each, teal #0072B2. Third box: exactly 3 bangles, amber #E69F00, and 1 empty space. Bangles are plain flat rings, all the same size. Below, centred: the sample equation, then the question in reddish purple #CC79A7. Exactly 3 boxes, 11 bangles.
rejection: any count of objects, cells, ticks or rows that differs from the numbers stated in the spec
any text beyond the listed visible text, or any listed text misspelled or altered
any board name, publisher name, book title, page number or curriculum branding anywhere in the frame
a hyphen used in place of a minus sign on any labelled number
a box holding more than 4 bangles, or any yes or no answer written
images.takeaway: A mixed number needs full boxes and some bangles left over.
images.description: Two full boxes of 4 teal bangles and a third box with 3 amber bangles show 11/4 = 2 3/4; the question asks whether a part is always left.
images.context: Shown with the concept as its one key picture, next to the walkthrough video. PLACEHOLDER: specified, not generated yet.
images.teaching_notes: Ask the student to think of a number of bangles that fills the boxes exactly and say what is left.

image_decisions.why: Boxes of four with a leftover make the whole part and fraction part visible, setting up the test.
